newToAA.heading: New to AA

whatIsAA.heading: What is AA?
whatIsAA.body: Alcoholics Anonymous is a fellowship of people who share their experience with each other to solve a common problem and help others recover from alcoholism. There are no dues or fees. The only requirement for membership is a desire to stop drinking.

whatHappens.heading: What happens at a meeting?
whatHappens.body: Meetings usually run about an hour. People share their own experiences — no one will call on you or ask you to speak. Some meetings are open to anyone; others are for people who have a drinking problem or think they might have one.

faq.a1: No. You're welcome to just listen.
faq.a2: AA doesn't keep attendance records or membership lists. What's said and who attends stays in the room.
faq.a3: No. AA has no dues or fees; it's self-supporting through voluntary contributions from members.
faq.q4: What's the difference between open and closed meetings?
faq.a4: Open meetings welcome anyone, including family or friends. Closed meetings are for those with a drinking problem, or who think they might have one.

newToAA.selfCheckPrompt: A short <link>self-check</link> can help you think this through — it isn't a diagnosis, and you don't need to take it before going to a meeting.

concernedAboutSomeone.heading: Concerned about someone
concernedAboutSomeone.intro: If someone you care about has a drinking problem, you're not alone, and it isn't yours to fix by yourself.

whatYouCanDo.heading: What you can do
whatYouCanDo.body: You can't make someone stop drinking. You can share that meetings exist, without pressuring them to go. Many people find it helps to talk to others who understand — Al-Anon is a separate fellowship specifically for the families and friends of people with drinking problems, if you'd like support of your own.

whereToStart.heading: If you're not sure where to start
whereToStart.body: You're welcome to call the helpline below and talk it through with someone.

howAAWorks.heading: How AA works
howAAWorks.body: AA has no leaders, no dues, and isn't affiliated with any religion, political group, or institution. Members follow the Twelve Steps, a set of principles for recovery, and the Twelve Traditions, which describe how AA groups stay unified and self-supporting.

selfCheck.heading: A few questions to think about
selfCheck.intro: There's no score and no right answer. This isn't a diagnosis — only you can decide what it means for you.
selfCheck.q1: Have you tried to cut back on drinking and found it harder than expected?
selfCheck.q2: Has anyone close to you said they're worried about how much you drink?
selfCheck.q3: Have you felt guilty or uneasy about your drinking?
selfCheck.q4: Do you ever need a drink to feel normal or steady in the morning?
selfCheck.q5: Has drinking gotten in the way of work, family, or things you care about?
selfCheck.q6: Do you drink alone, or hide how much you drink?
selfCheck.q7: Have you kept drinking even when it was clearly causing problems?
selfCheck.q8: Has drinking ever put you or someone else in a risky situation?

panel.default: Answer honestly, at your own pace — nothing here is scored or judged.
panel.resonates: It sounds like some of this might be familiar. Many people who feel this way find it helps to talk to someone or sit in on a meeting — there's no pressure, and no one will ask why you came.
